Asclepias quadrifolia is a slender eastern North American native named for the distinctive whorl of four leaves partway up its stem, producing small, fragrant, pale pink to white flower clusters in late spring that support native pollinators and serve as a larval host plant for monarch butterflies just as its sun-loving relatives do. Because it tolerates the light shade of an open woodland or forest edge, it fills a niche few other milkweeds can, making it a valuable addition to a shaded native pollinator garden or woodland-edge planting. It resents transplanting once its taproot is established, so start it from seed sown where it is to grow or move only small, young divisions.

Packera anonyma is a southeastern native forming a low mat of semi-evergreen, toothed basal leaves that sends up wiry stems topped with clusters of small, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers in late spring, providing early-season nectar for a range of small native bees and other pollinators. It tolerates dry, poor soil and light shade better than many groundcover perennials, making it useful for naturalizing along woodland margins, dry banks, and other tough sites where richer soil groundcovers struggle. It spreads readily by seed and short rhizomes to form a colony over a few seasons and needs essentially no supplemental care once established.

Coreopsis pubescens is a southeastern native with soft, downy, lance-shaped leaves and bright golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers with a darker center, blooming over a long season from early summer into fall and attracting a range of butterflies and native bees. Its tolerance for the dappled light of a woodland edge or the partial shade cast by taller perennials makes it a versatile choice for the transitional zone between a sunny border and a shaded planting. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.

Helianthus microcephalus is an eastern native perennial sunflower adapted to woodland edges and open forest understory, producing slender, branching stems and a profusion of small, delicate, pale yellow flower heads in late summer and fall that are an important late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies as sunnier flowers fade. Its shade tolerance and airy, small-flowered habit make it a good choice for naturalizing along a wooded property line or the high, filtered shade of mature trees where full-sun sunflower species will not thrive. It spreads by rhizome to form a colony over time and can be divided in spring to control its spread or share with other gardeners.

Lactuca canadensis is a tall, biennial-to-short-lived-perennial North American native related to cultivated lettuce, forming a basal rosette of deeply lobed leaves the first year and a towering flowering stalk topped with numerous small, pale yellow, dandelion-like flowers in late summer that draw bees, small butterflies, and seed-eating songbirds. Young spring leaves are edible and were traditionally eaten like garden lettuce, though they turn increasingly bitter as the plant matures and bolts toward flowering. It tolerates partial shade and a wide range of soils, making it a low-maintenance native for a woodland edge, pollinator meadow, or informal naturalized planting, though its height and reseeding habit suit an informal setting better than a tidy border.
